# Security, Credentials, and Data Privacy

## Overview
Automations often touch sensitive information - customer data, credentials, financial details - so security is a responsibility, not an afterthought, and getting it wrong can cause breaches, legal trouble, and lost trust. The most immediate concern is secrets management: API keys and tokens must be stored in your tool's secure credential manager or environment variables, never hard-coded in scripts, pasted into public channels, or committed to GitHub (reinforcing Day 21 and 28). If a secret leaks, rotate it immediately. The principle of least privilege means every credential and connection should have only the permissions it truly needs - if an automation only reads a spreadsheet, do not give it write access to your whole account - so that a compromised key does the least possible damage. You should minimize sensitive data: only collect and pass what you actually need, avoid logging personal data in plain text, and delete it when no longer required. Webhooks deserve special care because they are public URLs anyone could hit, so you validate incoming requests (using a secret token or signature) to ensure they really came from the expected source, preventing spoofed or malicious data from triggering your workflows. Finally, you need basic privacy awareness: regulations like GDPR govern how personal data (PII) may be collected, stored, and processed, and even as a beginner you should know not to move personal data carelessly across borders or services, to respect consent, and to be able to delete a person's data on request. You do not need to be a security expert, but building these habits - protect secrets, least privilege, minimize data, secure webhooks, respect privacy - marks you as a trustworthy engineer companies can safely hand real systems to.

## Deep Dive
This module covers: Managing API keys and secrets safely; Least privilege and scoped access; Encrypting and minimizing sensitive data; Secure webhooks and validating incoming data; Privacy basics (GDPR, PII) for automations. Mastering these ideas is essential because they appear repeatedly in production AI systems.

### What You Will Learn
- The core theory behind today's topic.
- How to apply it using Python, NumPy, Pandas, or the relevant framework.
- How to evaluate results and avoid common mistakes.
- Where to find authoritative references when you need deeper detail.

### Real-World Context
In industry, these skills are used daily: data scientists clean messy survey data, AI engineers deploy models to REST APIs, and automation engineers orchestrate pipelines. Today's practical task simulates one of these real-world scenarios.

## Hands-On Practice
Practical Task: Audit one of your automations for security: move any hard-coded secret into secure storage, reduce a connection's permissions to only what it needs, and add token validation to a webhook so only authorized requests are accepted.
Mini Project: Produce a security review of a workflow handling customer data: document where secrets live, what permissions each connection has, what PII is processed and why, how the webhook is validated, and a remediation for each weakness found.
Assignment: Explain the principle of least privilege with an automation example, and list five rules for handling API keys and personal data safely.

Complete all three sections. Each completed section earns points toward your CalibiAI Score. If you are unsure about any part, use the AI assessment popup to submit your work and receive dynamic feedback from DeepSeek.

## Common Mistakes to Avoid
Many beginners rush into coding before fully understanding the data. Others skip validation steps and overestimate model performance. This module helps you build the discipline of checking assumptions first, then applying algorithms systematically.

## Career Impact
The skills covered today are frequently tested in technical interviews and required in entry-level AI engineering roles. Building a portfolio that demonstrates mastery of these concepts will significantly improve your job prospects.

## Key Takeaways
1. Theory guides practice — understand before coding.
2. Clean data and clear metrics are more valuable than complex models.
3. Document your steps for reproducibility.
4. Communication matters: explain results to non-technical stakeholders.
